title: Factorial Calculator
story: Factorials grow shockingly fast. 5! = 120. 10! = 3,628,800. 20! = 2.4 quintillion. This explosive growth breaks programs if unchecked. Build a factorial calculator with overflow protection — contracts guard against the impossible.
why: Factorial calculations combine iteration with contract-based safety, demonstrating how contracts prevent silent failures from integer overflow.
analogy: Population growth: 2 people have 4 children, those 4 have 8, those 8 have 16 — but Earth can only support so many. Factorial is even faster than exponential growth. The contract is the 'carrying capacity' limit: beyond this point, everything breaks.
try_it: Try factorial(13) — observe the contract violation (or overflow if no contract). Add a second contract checking that result > previous factorial to catch overflows. Compute factorials as Float64 for larger n, but notice the precision loss.
tips: 0! = 1 by convention — this is the base case
Always bound factorial input — exponential growth breaks integers fast
Use contracts to catch impossible inputs at the call site, not inside the function
common_mistakes: Starting the loop at 1 instead of 2 — multiplying by 1 does nothing
Not adding overflow protection — silent bugs are the worst bugs
